newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown unveils radical maiden budget.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown unveils radical maiden budget.

text.p: Finance minister Gordon Brown unveiled a radical, tax-raising budget on Wednesday designed to cool Britain's sizzling economy, boost investment and gradually wipe out the government's budget deficit.
Brown told a packed House of Commons that the overarching theme of the first budget by a Labour government since 1979 was to provide "stability, investment, work and opportunity for all".
"The central purpose of this budget is to ensure that Britain is equipped to rise to the challenge of the new and fast-changing global economy. Not just a few of us, but everyone," he said.

Warning that rapid consumer spending risked sparking an unsustainable boom, Brown said he would raise an extra 5.5 billion pounds ($9.1 billion) in tax this year and 4.75 billion pounds next year to put Britain on the road to long-term financial stability.
"I will not ignore the warning signs and I will not repeat past mistakes," Brown, said. "This and future budgets will be addressed to laying the foundations for tomorrow's wealth."

To remedy Britain's poor investment record, which he said had lagged that of its main competitors since 1980, Brown cut the main rate of tax on company profits from 33 percent to a record low of 31 percent.
Arguing that small businesses in future will be the main engine of job creation, Brown also cut the tax rate on small companies to 21 percent from 23 percent.

In a further step to encourage firms to plough more profits back into investment instead of paying them out in dividends, Brown also said he was abolishing tax credits paid to pension funds -- estimated to be worth more than 3 billion pounds.

Brown confirmed that he was imposing a windfall tax of 5.2 billion pounds on the excess profits of utilities that Labour believes were privatised too cheaply by the previous Conservative administration.
He said the controversial tax would be sued to finance a "new deal" for 250,000 young jobless by offering them a "ladder of opportunity" into work.
The welfare-to-work programme, which also includes special measures to help single mothers back to work, would cost a total of 3.5 billion pounds, he said.
Brown, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, confirmed the new government's "green" credentials by announcing a tax break on buses and trucks that meet tough emission standards.

He also acted to take steam out of Britain's bubbling housing market by trimming the tax break homeowners get on mortgage interest payments and by increasing tax payable on purchases of expensive homes.

Brown responded to mounting complaints about Britain's cash-strapped health service by promising to take 1.2 billion pounds from the Treasury's contingency reserve next year to improve front-line patient care. ($ = 0.602 British Pounds)
